justification: Full independent technical pass: I re-implemented every algorithm myself under different names (SearchTree<T>/Tree<T>/PredTree<T>, Item/Node fields renamed) rather than copying the article's Bst<T>, and ran everything through `dotnet run <file>.cs` (.NET SDK 10.0.401) separately from the article's own harness. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/data-structures/binary-search-trees.md` from Git Bash: PASS, blocks=22 executed=11, byte-identical across 3 separate runs, and the tool's warning check (`if (/warning CS\d+/.test(all) ...)`) never fired on any block, confirming zero compiler warnings anywhere in the article -- meets the brief's 'no warnings' idiomatic-C# bar. Search/Insert/Contains: my SearchTree<T> reproduced Count=7, Contains(30)=True, Contains(45)=False, and duplicate-insert-is-no-op exactly. Delete, all three cases: my own leaf/one-child/two-child tests reproduced the article's exact outputs ('leaf after: 40', '1-child after: 10,40', '2-child after: 20,50,60' with Contains(50)=True), and I additionally tested a deeper two-child case the article's own code sample does not cover (successorParent != node, i.e. the successor is several levels below the deleted node's right child) and it worked correctly, plus deleting a non-existent key and deleting the root of a single-node tree. I then cross-checked both the successor-based Remove and the exercise's predecessor-based Remove against .NET's own `SortedSet<int>` as an oracle over 5,000 and 1,000 randomized insert/delete/remove-missing operations respectively (fixed seeds 123 and 55) -- zero mismatches in either direction, which is a stronger correctness check than the article's own worked examples give. Traversals: my independently-named PreOrder/PostOrder/InOrder analogs reproduced 'pre: 40,20,10,30,60,50,70' and 'post: 10,30,20,50,70,60,40' exactly. Degenerate-tree and height-measurement claims: I reproduced the article's exact table (seed 42, Fisher-Yates shuffle, sizes 500/2,000/8,000/30,000) and got randomH = 17, 23, 27, 33 -- identical to every digit in the article -- confirming the determinism claim is real, not asserted. I also ran the height experiment with a different seed (999) and different sizes (1,000/5,000/20,000), confirming sortedH always equals n-1 exactly (arithmetic, as the article says) and randomH stays in the 2.2-2.5x-of-minH band the article describes for its own range; I additionally pushed to n=1,000,000 across 5 trials each to sanity-check the 'expected height O(log n)' claim against the literature (Devroye 1986: height/ln(n) -> ~4.311 asymptotically) and found the measured ratio-to-minH climbing slowly (2.27 at n=1,000 to 2.62 at n=1,000,000) toward that larger asymptotic constant, exactly the well-known slow convergence of this quantity -- the article's own claim ('roughly two to two-and-a-half times the minimum-height column across the whole range') is correctly scoped to its measured range and does not overclaim an asymptotic constant, so this is not an error, just a note that the pattern is genuine and not cherry-picked. Rotations: I reproduced the exact before/after in-order sequences and the round-trip shape-equality exercise on a differently-shaped tree (root 100, not 20), then ran an independent stress test -- 2,000 random trees of size 3-14, rotating at the root whenever possible -- and got 0 in-order mismatches, which is a far stronger check of the 'rotation preserves in-order' claim than the single worked example. Red-black/BCL claims: I fetched SortedSet.cs, SortedSet.TreeSubSet.cs and SortedDictionary.cs directly from the dotnet/runtime main branch myself (not trusting the article's transcriptions). The four-rule red-black properties quote in the article matches the source's XML-doc comment character-for-character, including its slightly awkward phrasing ('If a node is red, the both its children are black'). `internal enum NodeColor : byte { Black, Red }` matches exactly. `RotateLeft`/`RotateRight` exist in the source with bodies structurally identical to the article's own (`Right = child.Left; child.Left = this;` vs. the article's `p.Right = q.Left; q.Left = p;` -- same operation, source's own variable names). The height-bound comment in the real source reads 'The maximum height of a red-black tree is 2 * log2(n+1). See page 264 of "Introduction to algorithms" by Thomas H. Cormen' -- the article states the same 2*log2(n+1) bound and correctly says only that '.NET's source cites [a proof] directly rather than re-deriving' it, without itself repeating CLRS's page 264, so the article does not inherit that unverifiable page-number citation. TreeSubSet's class summary -- 'This class represents a subset view into the tree. Any changes to this view are reflected in the actual tree' -- matches the article's quoted sentence verbatim, and I independently reproduced the live-view behavior with different years/values (2010-2019 view; adding 2012 and removing 2015 from the parent both show up in the view on next enumeration) exactly as the article's own GetViewBetween example does. SortedDictionary.cs's private field is confirmed `private readonly TreeSet<KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>> _set;`, matching the article's claim, and `TreeSet<T>`'s `AddIfNotPresent` override does throw `ArgumentException` on a duplicate rather than silently ignoring it, matching the article's characterization. MinInternal/MaxInternal are confirmed to walk the tree from the root on every access (no cached field) -- exactly the O(h) walk the article claims, not a claimed-but-unverified 'not cached' assertion. Both Microsoft Learn quotes were checked verbatim on the live pages: Dictionary<TKey,TValue>'s 'The order in which the items are returned is undefined' and SortedDictionary<TKey,TValue>'s 'is a binary search tree with O(log n) retrieval' -- both present, both in the Remarks section, neither clipped out of context. All 5 exercises verified by running independent re-implementations (different class/variable names) of each: predecessor-delete (matches article's before/after exactly, plus 0 mismatches over 1,000 randomized trials against SortedSet<int>), the buggy-post-order bug-find (buggy: 40,20,10,30,60; correct: 10,30,20,60,40 -- matches, and the diagnosis that the bug turns it into pre-order is correct), the reverse-sorted-insert height prediction (both height 6, in-order sequences equal -- matches), the rotation-round-trip proof (re-ran on a differently shaped 5-node tree, same-shape holds), and the Dictionary-vs-SortedDictionary comparison (re-ran with a different key set, SortedDictionary always ascending, matches an actual OrderBy exactly). CLRS citation restraint: grepped every 'CLRS' mention in the body (6 occurrences) -- all are chapter-level ('CLRS states...', "CLRS's binary-search-tree chapter...", 'CLRS proves...'), none carry a page number, satisfying EDITORIAL_BRIEF rule 3's restraint for uncited-page textbook claims. Front-matter chapter citations (4th ed., chapter 12 for Binary Search Trees, chapter 13 for Red-Black Trees) could not be independently re-confirmed for the specific 4th edition this session: MIT Press's own page still 403s to automated fetches (same failure the hash-tables round-1 review hit), and this session's web-search budget was exhausted before a definitive 4th-edition table-of-contents source was found. This mirrors exactly the unresolved-not-wrong gap the hash-tables critic flagged for CLRS chapter 11 (Hash Tables) in the same edition -- chapters 12/13 for BST/Red-Black Trees are the standard, widely-cited CLRS 3rd-edition numbering (Part III: 10 Elementary Data Structures, 11 Hash Tables, 12 Binary Search Trees, 13 Red-Black Trees, 14 Augmenting Data Structures) and the prior critic already established this numbering is widely cited as unchanged in the 4th edition, so I found no evidence of an error, only that I personally could not re-verify the 4th-edition-specific number this round either. No other factual error was found anywhere in the article: the O(h) cost bound for every BST operation, the three-delete-case argument (the successor/predecessor has at most one child by construction), the pre-order/post-order use cases (serialization/rebuild vs. bottom-up deletion or expression evaluation), the degenerate-tree argument, the rotation-is-O(1)-and-preserves-in-order argument, and the red-black-vs-hand-rolled-tree guidance in the closing section are all correct and precisely scoped (no unqualified 'always/never/only' claims that don't hold -- I checked every occurrence). This keeps the article well clear of both the factual-error cap (7) and the non-running-code cap (5); it is not scored higher only because of the one unresolved (not incorrect) CLRS-4th-edition chapter citation and one trivial quotation imprecision (see issues).

issues.location: "Inside SortedDictionary<TKey,TValue> and SortedSet<T>" section: "`TreeSet<T>` is declared as `sealed class TreeSet<T> : SortedSet<T>`"
issues.problem: The real declaration in SortedDictionary.cs (confirmed by direct fetch of the dotnet/runtime source) is `public sealed class TreeSet<T> : SortedSet<T>` -- the article's backtick-quoted declaration drops the `public` access modifier. It is presented as a near-verbatim code quotation (backticks, exact type/generic syntax) rather than a loose paraphrase, so a reader who checks the source against the quote will find it incomplete, even though nothing the article actually asserts about it (that it is sealed, derives from SortedSet<T>, and throws on duplicates) is wrong.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add the modifier back: `public sealed class TreeSet<T> : SortedSet<T>`.
